content: When using ORTHO TRI-CYCLEN® or ORTHO-CYCLEN® with the Sunday Start method, the first tablet should be taken on the first Sunday after the onset of menstruation. If menstruation begins on a Sunday, the first tablet should be taken on that same day. One active tablet is taken daily for 21 consecutive days, followed by one green inactive tablet daily for 7 days. After completing the 28-day cycle, a new course begins the following day, which will also be a Sunday. During the first cycle of the Sunday Start regimen, an additional contraceptive method should be used for the first 7 consecutive days of taking the tablets. For the Day 1 Start method, the initial cycle of ORTHO TRI-CYCLEN® or ORTHO-CYCLEN® begins with one active tablet taken daily starting on the first day of menstrual flow, which is considered Day 1. Active tablets are taken daily for 21 days, followed by one green inactive tablet daily for 7 days. The tablets are taken continuously without interruption for a total of 28 days. After completing the 28-day cycle, a new course begins the next day. When using ORTHO TRI-CYCLEN® for the treatment of acne, the dosing schedule should follow the same guidelines as its use as an oral contraceptive. The dosage regimen involves taking one active tablet daily for 21 days, followed by one green inactive tablet daily for 7 days. This regimen is available in a DIALPAK® Tablet Dispenser. After completing the 28-day cycle, a new course begins the next day. For further details on dosing, refer to the instructions for administration. The FDA package insert provides comprehensive information on oral contraceptive formulations, including indications, contraindications, side effects, drug interactions, precautions, overdose management, instructions for administration, and details on how the medication is supplied. It also includes pharmacokinetic and molecular data. Additional resources include online calculators for estimating creatinine clearance and converting patient weight from pounds to kilograms for accurate dosing. Publication resources provide access to recent articles, state-of-the-art reviews, and textbook information on oral contraceptive formulations. Trial resources include information on ongoing clinical trials and their results. Guidelines and evidence-based medicine resources include U.S. national guidelines, Cochrane Collaboration reviews, and cost-effectiveness analyses related to oral contraceptive formulations. Media resources offer educational materials such as slides, videos, images, podcasts, and MP3s. Patient resources include discussion groups, handouts, blogs, news updates, and marketplace information on oral contraceptive formulations. International resources are also available, including materials in Spanish.
